Margins over the best Sindhi-adapted baselines are small (0.002 fertility on FLORES+ at 64k), and we report no significance tests. A round-trip check finds no character loss for our tokenizer and silent character deletion (up to 0.85% of characters) in two existing ones; seven others lose less than 0.1%. We evaluate intrinsic metrics only, so effects on downstream tasks remain untested. Code and tokenizer files are public (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23962474).
author: Ali Nawaz, Muqadas Fareed, Soonh Sadaf

title: Can decision models extract clinical data from cancer pathology reports? An evaluation of accuracy, calibration, and failure modes
description:
arXiv:2611.20129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models are a new class of language model that, instead of generating text, choose one option per question from a fixed list and return a probability for every option. They have not yet been evaluated on clinical text. We evaluated two open-weights decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, for extracting 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports from a single centre, against a prospectively maintained clinical database. We compared them with two generative models: Qwen3.5 9B, run locally, and GLM-5.3-flash, run through a cloud API. Tev1 reached a mean field accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI 0.913 to 0.920), the same as Qwen3.5 9B (0.918; p = 0.26), and was four times faster (15 s against 61 s per report). Nimble reached 0.862 and GLM-5.3-flash 0.986. Both decision models matched GLM-5.3-flash on simple dichotomous categories. They were weak on measurements binned into categories, on fields whose correct answer was not reported, and on some complex decisions (e.g. involved margins). We found that the main cause of the inferior performance of Nimble's came from asking 25 questions in one request: with two questions per request, its accuracy improved. Pooled over fields, the returned probabilities were well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.022 and 0.026), but they did not flag systematic errors within single fields. A simulated strategy of sending answers with a probability below 0.94 to GLM-5.3-flash raised Tev1's accuracy to 0.982, with 38% of answers escalated. Decision models can extract explicitly stated findings from pathology reports quickly on local hardware and return useful probabilities. They should be validated in the configuration in which they will be used, restricted to the fields in which they are reliable, and combined with other methods for numeric values.
author: Indranil Mallick, Paromita Roy

title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.20144v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
author: Chirag Goel, Jacob Lavoie, Amirhossein Naghshzan, Jordan Bannister, Marzia Nouri, Mehar Bhatia, Matt Harris, Siva Reddy, Ars\`ene Fansi Tchango, Ga\'etan Marceau Caron

title: Rank, Don't Regress: A 279M Text Ranker Beats 2B and 7B VLMs on Referential Urdu GUI Grounding
description:
arXiv:2611.20145v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: UI grounding asks a model to find the screen element that a user instruction refers to. Most current systems use a vision-language model (VLM) that reads a screenshot and outputs pixel coordinates. We study this task on Urdu mobile web pages, a setting with no published UI grounding results. Instead of regressing coordinates, we take the candidate elements from the page DOM and train a 279M-parameter cross-encoder (mDeBERTa-v3-base) to pick one. The click point is the centre of the picked element's box, so it is exact whenever the right element is picked. We built a frozen test set of 304 instructions from six Urdu news sites; 149 of them (49%) are referential and never quote the full target text. Test domains were banned from training data before collection started. The ranker scores 73.4% point-in-box accuracy, against 29.6% for UI-TARS-2B and 23.7% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both zero-shot. On the referential slice the ranker scores 65.8%, against 30.2% for a string-matching baseline that needs no training. In a controlled comparison at small scale, with training data drawn from the same pages, a coordinate-regression model of similar size scores 1.6%. Adding element geometry as input tokens gives the best variant, at 75.7%. The ranker's errors concentrate in two places: elements that share identical text, and ordinal instructions such as "the fourth link".
author: Hamza Raziq Khan, Aimal Khan

title: Centered Ablation: Why Last-Layer Directional Ablation Under-Fires or Collapses, and a Closed-Form Fix
description:
arXiv:2611.20148v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Directional ablation removes a hidden state's component along a "behaviour direction" while a language model runs. It is the standard way to switch a behaviour such as refusal off, but it is erratic: on some models it barely fires, on others the text collapses into repetition. We show why, and fix it. At the last residual stream, ablation is exactly a logit bias: a fixed vocabulary footprint scaled by a gate, the cosine between the hidden state and the direction. The gate is measured from the origin, but last-layer states share a large common mode far from it, so a direction that overlaps the common mode fires on benign text and under-fires on its targets. Centered Ablation (CA) projects the common mode out of the direction, in closed form. Across 8 models, CA raises attack success by 29 and 46 points where the standard recipe under-fires, cuts collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50\% to 1\%, and preserves 12 to 40 points more benign answers on high-overlap models, 39 to 46 more than the affine offset of prior work. Two numbers computed before generation predict, on models the analysis had not seen, which gain faithfulness and which gain attack success, and a collapse index marks when text degenerates. We also show that two standard safety judges score collapsed text in opposite directions, which can fabricate a 46-point effect.
author: Quy-Anh Dang, Chris Ngo

title: Risk-certified prompt optimization for LLM-as-a-judge guardrails
description:
arXiv:2611.20156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge guardrails are often controlled primarily through system prompts, yet standard prompt optimization methods target average performance rather than explicit safety constraints. This paper studies system-prompt selection as a constrained optimization problem: maximize benign pass rate while keeping the missed-attack rate below a user-specified level {\alpha} with finite-sample statistical control. The framework combines LLM-based judging, automatic prompt generation, and distribution-free risk certification. This work instantiates it in two procedures: CPS and CRISP. CPS generates a fixed pool of prompts from training data, then certifies candidates on a held-out evaluation set using simultaneous upper confidence bounds and selects the certified prompt with the highest benign utility. CRISP instead integrates risk feedback into an adaptive search, using hard example-guided rewriting and a reusable-holdout interface to steer generation toward the feasible utility frontier. Experiments on four datasets covering prompt injection, system-prompt leakage, and sensitive-information disclosure show that risk-certified selection consistently respects the target missed-attack level on heldout tests, while utility improves as the permitted risk is relaxed. CRISP is especially useful when fixed-pool search fails to produce certifiable high-utility candidates.
author: Hussein Jawad, Alexandre Landeau, Guy Fleury Iradukunda, Paul Beaumont, Th\'eodore Rezel, Sofiane Schaack, Nicolas J-B. Brunel

title: Who Can You Hide Behind? Author-Conditioned Style Transfer and the Evasion of a Commercial AI-Text Detector
description:
arXiv:2611.20158v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI-text detectors can be sensitive to changes in writing style. We examined this sensitivity by rewriting 991 AI-generated answers with Gemini, using prompts that included a writing sample from one of 55 named authors. We scored each original and its rewrite with the QuillBot AI detector. The median score fell from 100% to 0%, and the mean fell from 67.9% to 11.2%. Of the rewrites, 66% received a score of exactly 0%. Among the 699 originals scored at least 50%, 71% of rewrites scored below 10% (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p-value below 1e-100). Scores varied across the authors used in the prompts. All rewrites associated with 10 authors scored 0%, whereas the mean score remained above 50% for six authors (Kruskal-Wallis test, p-value below 1e-80). Greater reuse of five-word sequences from the author sample was associated with lower scores, although rewrites with less than 5% reuse still averaged 15.2%. These results describe one detector and one rewriting system, not detectors in general. The study lacks a generic-rewrite baseline, did not measure preservation of meaning, and produced rewrites that were substantially longer than the originals.
author: Mohd Ruhul Ameen, M. Saifuzzaman Rafat, Akif Islam

title: Do We Still Need Fine-Tuned Classifiers? Swapping Typed Decision Models into 24 ACL-Venue Papers
description:
arXiv:2611.20191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed Decision Models such as TypeSafe's Jev, also called System One or System 1 models, answer typed questions about an input with a probability for each option, and they need no training. Many NLP papers still fine-tune a task-specific classifier, and prompted large language models (LLMs) trail such classifiers on most text classification benchmarks. We ask how many of these fine-tuned classifiers a Typed Decision Model can replace under each paper's own evaluation, and what is needed where it cannot. We swap the predictors of 24 ACL-venue papers for Jev, keep each paper's splits, label definitions and metric, and check the results with Cloudflare's Clef, Microsoft-Decision-1 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna Decisions. The resulting 46 English test sets, with their questions and published scores, form the TDM-Gauntlet benchmark. With a zero-shot prompt, Jev directly replaced the paper's predictor on 12 of the 46 test sets, mostly single judgments with plain labels, but rarely where the paper's method was trained on its labels. Where Jev scored lower, we most often attributed the shortfall to an annotation convention that the label name does not state. With 500 training labels plus validation and no user-managed GPU, calibration and GEPA-style prompt optimization closed a median 72% of the gap to the paper's method, about twice what off-the-shelf GEPA closed, for a median $1.66 per search. On the same labels, fine-tuned encoders such as RoBERTa and DeBERTa closed 59%, and LoRA fine-tuning of the open LLM Qwen3.8-27B closed 97%. Fine-tuning remains the most accurate option, but a zero-shot prompt is often enough for plain labels, and prompt optimization closes most of the remaining gap.
author: Marek \v{S}uppa, Jaroslav Kop\v{c}an

title: FIDEL: Abugida-Aware Pre-tokenization for Ethiopic Languages
description:
arXiv:2611.20216v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Subword tokenizers assume that meaningful linguistic units can be recovered by splitting text at learned boundaries, an assumption better suited to concatenative morphology than to Semitic root-and-pattern systems. The challenge is acute for the Ethiopic languages, whose abugida script encodes consonant-vowel units as single characters and hides consonantal structure. We introduce FIDEL (FId\"al DEcomposition and Linearization), a family of reversible abugida-aware pre-tokenization schemes that expose consonant and vowel-order structure, extend SPLINTER reductions from abjad scripts to the Ethiopic abugida, and evaluate them on three Ethiopic languages under controlled conditions, holding corpus, architecture, budget and protocol fixed so that tokenization is the only variable. We report intrinsic tokenizer statistics for BPE and UnigramLM across vocabulary sizes alongside downstream NLP tasks, including transfer scenarios. We find that FIDEL reduction improves news classification consistently and named-entity recognition at larger capacity, while sentiment analysis performance declines under the more aggressive schemes, and extractive question answering performance is preserved.
author: Gebreslassie Teklu Reda, Yuval Pinter

title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
description:
arXiv:2611.20230v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.
author: J\"urgen Paulhart ([core] Informationstechnologie / Eldric), Peter Sch\"uller (NeuraMix AI GmbH,Technische Universit\"at Wien)

title: Hochschild Cocycle and Universality of Merge
description:
arXiv:2611.20305v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Hopf algebra Markov chain dynamical system, on the Hopf algebra of non-planar binary forests, that models the action of Merge on workspaces in Chomsky's Minimalist Model of syntax, satisfies a universal property, determined by the fact that the Merge operation is a Hochschild 1-cocycle. This universal property has an interpretation in terms of models of the syntax-semantics interface, as it shows that, if the side of semantics possesses a sufficiently rich compositional structure, then that structure is uniquely induced by the syntactic Merge, once the semantic values of lexical items and syntactic features are assigned. We illustrate how this universality works by showing, in particular, full compatibility of this Hopf algebraic formulation with Heim-Kratzer semantics.
author: Matilde Marcolli, Elizabeth Xiao

title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
description:
arXiv:2611.20335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.
author: Fangzhi Li, Quan Shi, Wenting Yang, Yueqiao Chen, Jiayu Chang, Shuting Zhao, Zhaowei Xu, Yizhao Chen, Guanchu Wu, Han Xu

title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.20398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.
author: Yiwei Fu, Nicholas Gabriel

title: Refusal Register is Causally Steerable: Decomposing the Refusal Direction into Category-Aligned Components in Gemma-2-9B-IT
description:
arXiv:2611.20405v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prior work shows that refusal in instruction-tuned language models can be ablated by intervening on a single residual-stream direction (Arditi et al., 2024), and more recent work finds multiple refusal-mediating directions and concept cones (Wollschl\"ager et al., 2025). We ask a different question: do refusal-related directions carry information about the register of refusal language - how the model refuses - and not only whether it refuses? In Gemma-2-9B-IT we identify two SVM-derived linear directions (B1 for harmful-content vs. neutral, B2 for self-reference vs. neutral) at layer 20 with cos(B1, B2) = 0.252 (about 75 degrees, substantially non-parallel). Adding the harmful-vs-neutral difference-of-means direction (cosine 0.68 with B1) to the residual stream of self-reference prompts at alpha = 2.0 shifts content-safety vocabulary from 2.55 to 10.37 hits per 100 tokens, while a magnitude-matched random direction produces 1.13-2.16; the model continues to refuse but switches register from meta-style ("as a language model...") to content-style ("this would be harmful"). The same register-injection effect reproduces qualitatively in Gemma-2-2B-IT at layer 12 (content vocabulary 1.72 -> 6.37 at alpha = 1.0, vs. random control 1.35), with a narrower coherent-injection window than in 9B. The two directions are not symmetric: the B2 -> harmful intervention produces a much smaller register effect, and across ablation, sufficiency, and injection B1's causal effects are consistently larger than B2's. We frame this asymmetry as part of the finding: B1 appears to encode both category detection and refusal-vocabulary information, while B2 encodes primarily category detection. We frame the contribution as identifying category-aligned components related to the Arditi-style difference-of-means direction that play distinct functional roles in refusal register.
author: Janhavi Khindkar, Nataliia Povarova

title: Augmenting Pretrained Language Models with N-gram Embeddings through Incremental Training
description:
arXiv:2611.20415v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.
author: Shaohua Hu, Xusheng Gu, Haofei Yang, Minghao Shao, Nanhui Zhao, Caoyun Fan, Fangming Li

title: A Structural Framework for Succession: Continuation, Recognition, and Realization
description:
arXiv:2611.20422v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Succession asks whether an entity encountered later is the same entity that entered an arrangement earlier. For an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied, it has to be answered. We look for a mathematical structure weak enough to cover any such case and strong enough to support general theorems, so that results follow from the structure's conditions rather than from a particular pipeline or criterion. Succession is modeled on state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths. Within this framework we separate four questions that are often conflated: which continuations a representation admits, which descendants are compatible with a modification, which are recognized as continuing the identity, and which are realized. The framework allows one to address systematically questions of symmetry, computational complexity, recoverability, and robustness to partial realization, and we establish what the structure settles in each case before any particular criterion of identity is chosen.
author: Ilya A. Shkrob

title: FinVerify: A Verification Framework for Financial Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20423v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial agents produce numerical claims that can be wrong even when their calculations execute correctly, due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions. We introduce FinVerify, an evidence-grounded framework for verifying financial agents' numerical claims. Based on an analysis of 190 incorrect trajectories from the Agent Finance Reasoning dataset, we define five error categories--temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, and financial-model fidelity--and operationalize them as verification protocols. An LLM structures claims and supporting evidence, while deterministic validators check financial requirements; when authoritative formulas are available, Z3 checks consistency with grounded inputs. FinVerify accepts only if all applicable checks pass, rejects proven violations, and abstains when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate the framework against a Direct baseline and an LLM judge across five fixed-candidate benchmarks. On Agent Finance Reasoning, accepted-claim precision increases from 56.4% for the LLM judge to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage. On XBRLFiling, FinVerify achieves 99.8% accepted-claim precision and 97.0% decision accuracy; on FinanceBench-67, it reaches 87.9% accepted-claim precision versus 69.7% for the judge. Improvements are smaller on FinQA and TAT-QA, where authoritative evidence is limited. These results suggest that explicit, evidence-backed verification can improve financial-agent reliability while exposing trade-offs between correctness, false rejection, and abstention.
author: Mao Guan, Qian Chen, Ge Meng, Xiao-Yang Liu

title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.20441v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.
author: Koki Itai, Jun Hirako, Hiroaki Yamagiwa

title: The Logic Chain Breaking Point: A Controlled-Variable Benchmark for Reasoning Degradation in Open-Weight Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.20447v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.
author: Akif Islam, Mohd. Ruhul Ameen, Md. Ekramul Hamid

title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
description:
arXiv:2611.20484v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics.
  We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.
author: Cong Wang, Qiaoyi Zheng, Zhaoguo Wang, Fan Long

title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20488v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.
author: Yerin Nam, Minkyung Cho, MinKyu Kim, SeungWoo Song, Hangyeol Yoo, Jihyo Kim, KyungTae Lim

title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.20535v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.
author: Hongbo Zhang, Liuyang Song, Hang Zhou, Xinchen Liu, Wei He, Kai Han, Yunhe Wang

title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
description:
arXiv:2611.20566v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.
author: Makoto Sato

title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20569v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.
author: Ke Shen, Ankita Bhaumik, Li Dong, Shengjie Liu, Shuzhen Li, Naveed Ahmed Janvekar

title: Dynamic Shaping: Acquiring Interfaces and Constructing Execution over Frozen Pretrained Components
description:
arXiv:2611.20573v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Dynamic Shaping, a method for constructing executable neural arrangements through acquired response and partial-derivative interfaces over frozen pretrained components. The method learns local descriptions of available computation, ranks component rebindings using task-gradient alignment, transports the current interface across a rebinding, and retains changes through behavioral feedback. Continuous interface acquisition uses proximal policy optimization; the source coefficients remain fixed. We derive an exact identity relating transport error in component responses and partials to changes in action logits and their sensitivities. A pixels-only ViZDoom Basic study evaluates first task acquisition without a competent reference controller, demonstrations or intact response targets. Across three initializations and 100 shared held-out game seeds, initial arrangements succeed on 86/300 controller/episode pairs; joint interface-and-binding construction succeeds on 295/300. Fixed-binding interface acquisition also reaches 295/300. Each policy executes four source fragments, with 110 acquired interface values and fixed random visual and action projections. The artifact includes all candidate trials, interventions and costs; all 1,200 recorded initial/retained outcomes replay exactly. The contribution is an explicit profile, rebind, transport and retain procedure and a reproducible reference-free acquisition case over frozen pretrained computation.
author: Nathaniel Oh

title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
description:
arXiv:2611.20579v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.
author: Jun Wu, Deming Li, Zhenming Zheng, Honghao Yue, Fei Yang, Hao Sun

title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
description:
arXiv:2611.20595v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.
author: Sajib Acharjee Dip, Brian Ouyang, Lala Motlhabi

title: BiGSyn: A Bi-Level Heterogeneous Graph Contrastive Learning Framework for Interpretable Drug Synergy Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.20603v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy, providing interpretable insights.
author: Senquan Wang, Hui Fang, Haoran Nan, Xingwei Wang, Qiang He

title: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.
author: Runzhe Wang, Huilin Lu, Shengjie Liu, Li Dong, Zhihuai Zhu

title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
description:
arXiv:2611.20608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.
author: Jizhou Guo

title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual
description:
arXiv:2611.20616v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).
author: Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu, Ji Liu

title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
description:
arXiv:2611.20643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.
author: Ruoxuan Shi, Sheng Yang, Zhengxing Su, Xiaoyang Hou, Yating Liu

title: MetaAct: Self-Evolving Executable Action Constraints for Embodied Language Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.
author: Jiaxing Zhao, Hanwen Wang, Di Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Jing-Ran Su, Yanheng Li, Qian Zha, Jiaxi Li, Hongbin Xie, Haoran Zhang, Xuan Song, Haoxuan Che

title: LEAF-OPD: Learning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.20674v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.
author: Zirui Pang, Zhijie Deng, Yuancheng Wang, Qihan Yu, Xin Li, Jiaheng Wei, Zixin Zhong

title: UbiHearo: Bringing Scenario-Aware Sound Guidance to DHH Users with Mobile Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) users, effective sound awareness goes beyond detecting \emph{what} sound occurs; it requires understanding \emph{what it means}, \emph{how urgent it is}, and \emph{what to do}. However, existing mobile assistants largely reduce acoustic scenes to isolated labels or generic alerts, failing to provide contextual guidance when the same sound implies different risks across scenarios. We present \sysname, a mobile hearing assistant agent that closes the sensing--reasoning--action loop for \textit{scenario-aware} and \textit{personalized} DHH assistance. \sysname adopts a \textit{neuro-symbolic} design that transforms continuous acoustic and physical context streams into structured intermediate representations (IRs) for controllable reasoning and guidance. It introduces three key mechanisms. \textit{First}, a perception-thresholded sensing mechanism enables energy-efficient always-on awareness by activating processing only for perceptually meaningful events while preserving safety-critical cues through deterministic overrides. \textit{Second}, a staged neuro-symbolic reasoning framework performs promptless scenario understanding by conditioning an on-device audio-language model on structured IRs instead of user-authored context descriptions. \textit{Third}, a bounded human-in-the-loop personalization mechanism adapts user-specific guidance through lightweight on-device decision-boundary updates while preserving population-aligned reasoning. We evaluate \sysname on smartphones and in-vehicle systems across diverse scenarios. It achieves favorable accuracy--latency--energy tradeoffs and personalized guidance.
author: Fengmin Wu, Sicong Liu, Zimu Zhou, Chenren Xu, Wanbing Zhao, Peiwen Sun, Zhiwen Yu

title: VIVID: A Visual Harness for Agentic Video Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.20688v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video editing requires agents to make editing decisions grounded in audiovisual observations and precise temporal localization, and to evaluate their effects in rendered outputs. General-purpose coding agents possess strong comprehension, reasoning, and code execution capabilities, while media interaction and evidence management mechanisms tailored to video tasks can further unlock their editing potential. We introduce VIVID, a visual harness that supports multiple native coding agents in video post-production without additional model training. VIVID provides tools for on-demand video inspection, audio analysis, and transcription, and preserves observations alongside their corresponding media versions and temporal coordinates. Agents can actively retrieve these observations as they reason, perform edits using their native coding and shell tools, and inspect rendered outputs to guide subsequent revisions. On AgenticVBench, comprising 100 tasks across Assembly, Repair, Sequencing, and Repurpose, Codex with VIVID achieves an average score of 58.6%, an improvement of 20.2 percentage points over native Codex. The same harness also integrates with Claude Code and OpenCode, achieving average scores of 55.1% and 37.1%, respectively, both substantially exceeding their native baselines. These results highlight VIVID's potential as a reusable visual harness for extending the capabilities of general-purpose coding agents to video editing.
author: Wenhan Yu, Zhaoxi Zhang, Zhilong Tan, Weikang Li, Lei Sha

title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.20693v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
author: Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang

title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.20695v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at: https://github.com/J4cksonLee/IndKnow
author: Haiteng Wang, Haoze Li, Jingwei Guo, Jingbo Zhou, Si Liu, Lei Ren

title: AgentFaultBench: State-Verified Evaluation of Tool-Fault Recovery
description:
arXiv:2611.20711v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does recovery advice help an agent finish a task after a tool fails? AgentFaultBench evaluates LangGraph and CrewAI agents performing specified tasks in an isolated GitLab installation. We inject tool errors and check both the resulting files and issues and the required reads, verification and final response. The prompt supplies the expected issue and report text, so the task tests execution rather than content generation. In the primary comparison of 1,944 planned runs, advice changes success by -8.33, 0.00 and +1.06 percentage points relative to a neutral reminder; missing outcomes leave the latter two comparisons inconclusive. Later experiments test a revised recovery policy. GPT-4o mini improves, while Sol and Claude already complete the recoverable cases. In a separate 624-run study on six related tasks not previously used by that policy, the guided condition records 161 correct final states and one unknown outcome in 192 planned runs, versus 142/192 with neutral feedback. The gain lies between +9.90 and +10.42 pp when missing outcomes are included. Removing issue IDs gives 47/48 successes versus 46/48 with IDs; other execution information remains. A second checker agrees on 1,879 observed primary outcomes and 241 constructed test cases. No human validation was collected. The findings support testing advice against explicit recovery controls rather than assuming it helps.
author: Sachin Gupta

title: PEETS: Preference-aware Embeddings with Explicit Tree Structure for Auxiliary Product Bundling
description:
arXiv:2611.20726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Auxiliary products such as flight protection and flexible-change services are recommended alongside primary travel purchases. This setting creates a granularity ambiguity: SKUs within one product type share semantics but differ in price and coverage, while rejecting one offer does not imply disinterest in the entire type. We present \textbf{PEETS} (\textbf{P}reference-aware \textbf{E}mbeddings with \textbf{E}xplicit \textbf{T}ree \textbf{S}tructure), a training-time framework for auxiliary product bundling. PEETS regularizes an existing click--conversion predictor through two conditional comparisons. Hierarchical Contrastive Loss uses the pair's common ancestor as a reference; Negative Contrastive Loss conditions structural sampling and comparison shifts on logged rejection events. Both act on shared SKU representations during training. This separates catalog relatedness from individual preference supervision and leaves the predictive serving path intact. PEETS achieves 78.20\% AUC, exceeding TWIN V2 by 0.90 percentage points and the matched base model by 1.15 points. In a 14-day online evaluation, gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day improves by 8.20\% over Policies, 3.06\% over Base, and 0.84\% over TWIN V2, with all three user-bootstrap 95\% intervals above zero. Bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies. The cancellation interval's upper limit exceeds the prespecified margin. PEETS adds no auxiliary-loss computation to serving and records 42.1~ms p95 latency, compared with 42.0~ms for Base.
author: Maolei Huang, Jing Tian, Dexuan Duan, Yan Chen, Huawei Cao, Shuhan Song

title: ANCHOR: Cluster-Grounded 5W1H Extraction via Large-Small Model Collaboration
description:
arXiv:2611.20728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep semantic understanding of events requires recognizing related events and distinguishing why an event occurs from how it is carried out. 5W1H extraction provides a structured foundation for such understanding by organizing event information around six fundamental questions. However, single-event slot filling provides limited support for these distinctions. We propose ANCHOR, a cluster-grounded framework that combines a large language model (LLM) with a small language model equipped with discriminative heads for accurate 5W1H extraction. The LLM proposes candidate events and generates their initial 4W records, which guide the selection of an event cluster and the subsequent anchoring of its main event. A shared document encoder provides evidence for joint 4W refinement, and two separate sets of boundary and role-scoring heads then extract why and how under event-specific constraints, respectively. Document representations are reused across events and stages, and unsupported roles can remain empty. Following the same principles, an agent-and-skill annotation workflow constructs a benchmark of 26,110 documents from ten source corpora covering three languages and seven domains. We select nine of the resulting datasets to evaluate ANCHOR against strong baselines using four open-weight LLMs. ANCHOR achieves competitive performance. The datasets and code are available at https://github.com/revolution6575/ANCHOR-5W1H.
author: Hongyu Jiang, Chenang Cai, Lei Gao, Zhao Kang, Ling Tian, Jinchuan Zhang

title: Routing Beyond Task Categories: A Cost-Aware LAB-Bench Study
description:
arXiv:2611.20732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We tested whether features of biology questions or of a model's first answer can improve accuracy within an inference budget. In a LAB-Bench pilot, we compared a category router with one that adds six structural features. Neither reached the primary 80% accuracy target on development. At the 50% and 60% secondary targets, both chose Haiku for all 120 held-out questions and scored 71/120. We then froze a new comparison before collecting responses on 144 additional questions. Semantic routing scored 86/144. A policy that could defer after reading Haiku's answer scored 87/144. Both stayed within the inference budget of USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries. Against a 95% Haiku and 5% GPT mixture, the accuracy gains were 0.66 percentage points for semantic routing and 1.35 points for deferral. The paired 95% intervals were [-0.28,2.25] and [-0.14,3.47] points. A simple rule that escalated Haiku nonanswers scored 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries, above the budget. A retrospective nonanswer rule with a calibration-selected escalation probability gave an expected 85.63/144. At the learned deferral policy's observed inference cost, post hoc interpolation gave an expected 86.14/144. In a later development check, Astra and Gemini each scored 30/40. The best tested policy in each router family matched that score. The pair covered 33/40 in hindsight. The routers missed the 32/40 criterion, so the proposed 120-question evaluation did not start.
author: Ahmed Tariq (Independent researcher), Leo Guinan (Idea Nexus Ventures)

title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.20733v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.
author: Peng Liu, Zhen Tao, Jihao Zhao, Ding Chen, Yansong Zhang, Cuiping Li, Zhiyu Li, Hong Chen

title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
description:
arXiv:2611.20734v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.
author: Assaf Hallak, Yftah Ziser, Gal Chechik

title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.20736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.
author: Kangwen Zhao, Jianfeng Cai, Ruopei Sun, Mingxiao Feng, Peng Zhang, Wengang Zhou, Houqiang Li

title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
description:
arXiv:2611.20755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.
author: Zifan Zhang, Zhengbo Jiao, Shaobo Wang, Jing Zhou, Guoyi Li, Jiayi Chen, Wei Wang, Bing Zhao, Cheng Fang, Xiaoxiao Xu, Hu Wei, Linfeng Zhang, Lin Qu

title: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.20759v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.
author: Manan Suri, Dinesh Manocha

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.20771v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.
author: NVIDIA,  :, Adi Margolin, Aditya Malte, Aishwarya Chhabra, Alex Hodson, Ameya Sunil Mahabaleshwarkar, Ambrish Dantrey, Amy Shen, Andrii Skliar, Annamalai Chockalingam, Anusha Pant, Ashwath Aithal, Ashwin Kumar, Besmira Nushi, Bhavesh Pawar, Bryan Catanzaro, Bryan Yu, Chantal Hwang, Chenhan Yu, Chris Alexiuk, Conner Currie, Cynthia Gao, David Mosallanezhad, Dina Yared, Ehsan Hosseini Asl, Eileen Long, Erick Galinkin, Felix Friedmann, Giedrius Burachas, Gorkem Batmaz, Grzegorz Chlebus, Guillermo Siman, Haifeng Qian, Hao Guo, Hayley Ross, Hrishith Thadicherla, Hui Wang, Huiying Li, Ike Nnoli, Irina Filatova, Iris Liu, Ji-Eun Lee, Jian Leong, Jian Zhang, Jiaqi Zeng, Joey Conway, Jonathan Cohen, Jose Vergara, Julien Veron Vialard, Kari Briski, Katherine Luna, Kedar Pandurang Potdar, Kevin Ning, Khalil Ben Khaled, Krzysztof Pawelec, Laura Dykes, Leili Tavabi, Lily Lee, Linda Liu, Liwei Ding, Maka Dong, Manoj Kilaru, Maria Bagdasarova, Matthew Lee, Meredith Price, Micah Schaffer, Michael Boone, Michael Fukuyama, Michael Hasper, Nancy Agarwal, Negar Habibi, Oleksii Kuchaiev, Oluwatobi Olabiyi, Pablo Ribalta, Payal Motwani, Pinky Xu, Prasoon Varshney, Pritam Biswas, Puhui Meng, Rameshwar Shivbhakta, Ran Zilberstein, Reka Kovacs, Richard Mazzarese, Rishabh Garg, Rita Fernandes Neves, Rochelle Woods, Ruby Ye, Ruvaid Virk, Ryan Hill, Saeid Motiian, Seph Mard, Shai Ben Nun, Shaona Ghosh, Sharad Yadav, Sudeep Sabnis, Suhas Hariharapura Sheshadri, Terry Kong, Thanh Do, Thinh Le, Udi Karpas, Viet Anh Trinh, Vinay Raman, Vinita Sharma, Warren Drones, Wenwen Gao, Whei Hsueh, Will Efstratis, Yoshi Suhara, Yunsheng Liu, Zhenming Wang, Zijia Chen, Zuhair Ahmed

title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.20779v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification.
